analysis.one_liner: Restores employer liability for workplace harassment by supervisors who direct workers' daily jobs.
analysis.headline: The bill to overturn the Supreme Court's Vance v. Ball State harassment ruling won 62 cosponsors, all Democrats, but was referred to four committees and never received a hearing, markup, or vote before the 113th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: In 2013 the Supreme Court ruled in Vance v. Ball State University that employers can only be held automatically responsible for harassment by a 'supervisor' who has the power to hire, fire, or demote an employee — not by someone who merely controls that employee's day-to-day work. This bill would change federal law so that employers are liable when harassment comes from anyone authorized to direct an employee's daily work, or when the employer's own negligence allowed a hostile workplace to form or continue. It would apply across the major federal anti-discrimination laws, including for federal employees and Congressional staff.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers harassed on the job — especially low-wage workers in retail, restaurants, health care, housekeeping, and farming, where many harassers direct daily work but cannot hire or fire. The bill's findings note that a quarter of working women report experiencing sexual harassment and that 80 percent of female farmworkers surveyed in central California reported experiencing it. It would also cover federal employees and Congressional staff under the same standard.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Harassed workers, especially in low-wage jobs

how_it_helps.text: Makes employers automatically liable for harassment by anyone authorized to direct an employee's daily work activities or to undertake or recommend tangible employment actions, and for harassment that continues because of the employer's own negligence.

Applies the standard across Title VII of the Civil Rights Act, the Age Discrimination in Employment Act, the Americans with Disabilities Act, the Rehabilitation Act, the Genetic Information Nondiscrimination Act, and protections for federal employees and Congressional staff.
Would apply to all claims pending on or after enactment, so workers whose cases were narrowed by the Supreme Court's ruling could benefit.

analysis.who_pays: Employers — businesses, and federal employing offices including Congress itself — who would face broader legal liability, larger settlements, and stronger incentives to prevent and correct harassment. Section 12 explicitly preserves all existing employer defenses, so the change is limited to who counts as a supervisor.

drawbacks.text: Broader liability raises the cost of defending and settling harassment claims for businesses of all sizes, including small employers, which opponents argued would push firms toward quick settlements rather than defending against weak claims.

The bill preserves the employer's ability to assert existing defenses, but by expanding who counts as a supervisor it increases the number of situations in which an employer is liable even after exercising reasonable care to prevent harassment.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For workers, the benefit is direct: it restores the pre-2013 understanding that a boss who controls your shifts and daily assignments can make your workplace hostile, and that the employer answers for it. The cost falls on employers as greater liability, which is the point — it creates a financial incentive to police harassers. The bill is drafted narrowly, keeping all existing employer defenses, but it does widen litigation exposure and could increase settlement pressure on employers regardless of claim strength.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to four House committees and three subcommittees, but none of them ever held a hearing or vote on it, and it died when the 113th Congress ended in January 2015.

narrative.text: Rep. George Miller introduced the bill on March 13, 2014, with 24 original cosponsors, and 62 House Democrats eventually cosponsored it.
It was referred to the Education and the Workforce, House Administration, Judiciary, and Oversight and Government Reform committees, and later to three subcommittees.
No further action — no hearing, markup, committee vote, or floor vote — was ever taken, and the bill expired when the Congress ended on January 3, 2015.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers came out ahead: the narrower liability standard from Vance v. Ball State University remained the law, leaving harassed workers — particularly low-wage workers whose harassers direct their daily work but cannot hire or fire — with harder cases to bring.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Employers who keep the narrower liability standard

for.name: Rep. George Miller
for.role: U.S. Representative (CA-7), senior Democrat on Education and the Workforce; bill sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Fair Employment Protection Act of 2014 and recruited 24 original cosponsors.

against.name: House committee chairs (Education and the Workforce, Judiciary, House Administration, Oversight)
against.role: Chairs of the four committees the bill was referred to
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing or markup on the bill during the 113th Congress.

against.name: Business and employer groups
against.what_they_did: Opposed legislative overrides of the Vance v. Ball State liability standard, arguing it would expand employer liability for harassment.

sides.party_line_note: All 62 cosponsors were Democrats and the sponsor was a Democrat; no Republican cosponsored, and the Republican-led committees never acted on the bill.

industries.industry: Employers in low-wage, high-harassment industries (retail, restaurants, hospitality, health care, housekeeping, farming)
industries.note: Because the Vance ruling narrowed who counts as a supervisor, employers in industries where shift leads control daily work but cannot hire or fire face less liability for harassment. The bill's own findings highlight that workers in these industries are especially vulnerable, so leaving the ruling intact protects employers from the lawsuits this bill would have revived.

industries.industry: Federal government and Congress as employers
industries.note: The bill would have applied the same liability standard to federal agencies and Congressional employing offices, including under the Congressional Accountability Act, so these employers would bear the same expanded liability as private firms.
